question: Which statement best describes unknown?
options: Use a type check before reading an error’s properties. `value instanceof Error` recognizes ordinary JavaScript `Error` objects. It is like checking a package label before following its instructions. Some libraries throw custom values, so decide how your application handles those cases instead of assuming every failure has a `.message` field. For example, use a type check before reading a property from an unknown caught value. For example, use a type guard before reading a message property.

`unknown` means a value exists but its type has not been safely established. Unlike `any`, TypeScript will not let you use it freely. It is like a sealed package that you must inspect before opening. In a `catch` block, begin with `unknown` because code can throw strings, objects, or other unexpected values. For example, an API helper may throw a string, so a catch block cannot assume every value has a message. For example, a library may reject a promise with a string instead of an Error object.

Convert unexpected failures into a message your application can safely display. A fallback such as “Something went wrong” is clearer than showing `[object Object]`. This is like translating an unclear report into a useful status. Keep the original value for controlled diagnostics where possible, while handling formatting without crashing again. For example, a safe fallback message keeps an error screen readable when the thrown value is unusual. For example, show users a safe summary while recording controlled diagnostics for developers.

Do not show stack traces, file paths, or raw server responses to ordinary users. They can expose implementation details or private data. Think of the stack trace as a repair log for the maintenance team, not a public sign. Give users a helpful next step and record detailed diagnostics in an access-controlled system. For example, keep a request identifier in diagnostics while omitting tokens and private payloads. For example, do not include tokens or private response bodies in the diagnostic context.
